reconcile.note: Adam Clarke limits Paul's ban on fellowship with unbelievers to idolatrous worship and apostasy, not the ordinary social contact that the love-your-neighbor texts require.

discrepancy.note: Ingersoll presses the same Bible's love-neighbor command against Deuteronomy 13's order to kill an enticing kinsman, calling it a book with no toleration for unbelief.

quotes.text: Within the Old Testament there is no such thing as religious toleration. Within that volume can be found no mercy for an unbeliever.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (Rejoinder to Judge Black) (1881), on Deuteronomy 13.

quotes.text: for one who follows the Master who said that when smitten on one cheek you must turn the other, and who again and again enforced the idea that you must overcome evil with good, it is hardly consistent to declare that a civilized nation must of necessity adopt the warfare of savages.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (Rejoinder to Judge Black) (1881), on Matthew 5:44.

quotes.text: In the presence of these commandments, what becomes of the fine saying, "Love thy neighbor as thyself"?
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (Rejoinder to Judge Black) (1881), on Leviticus 19:18.

sides.verseText: but you shall surely kill him; your hand shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterwards the hand of all the people.
But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,
